MFF KD phenotype, suggesting ARP2/3 is downregulated by MFF to support fission. Again, making a
conclusion based on one inhibitor data is problematic. Knocking down or out ARP2/3 can be attempted.
Response: To further clarify the mechanism by which MFF may promote early melanosome fission,
we followed the reviewer’s suggestion and investigated the role of the ARP2/3 complex in
melanosome morphology by siRNA. We performed knockdown experiments targeting two ARP2/3
subunits, ARPC1A and ARPC3, and observed an increase in melanosome size in both cases,
phenocopying the effects of Mff knockdown (Fig. 5G). Importantly, MFF puncta remained detectable
at early-stage melanosomes under these conditions, indicating that the recruitment of MFF is
independent of the ARP2/3 complex. This supports our model in which MFF may interact with ARP2/3
regulators to specifically drive fission (Fig. 5H). To further support the idea that MFF and actin could
cooperate to control melanosome membrane dynamics, we performed additional microscopy
experiments. We found that F-actin is enriched at melanosome fission sites marked by MFF (Fig. 5C,
D), strengthening our hypothesis that MFF-dependent melanosome fission is mediated by actin
nucleation factors.
8. lines 267, it would be better to discuss the genetic causes of the diseases and see if any is linked to
fission or MFF deficiency.
Response: We appreciate this suggestion, however, the involvement of MFF in skin physiology has
never been explored before, and we could not find any relevant data or literature. Moreover, the MFF
KO mouse is not viable. We believe that due to the impact of MFF deletion in other tissues, the effects
in skin may have been overlooked.
9. Fig 1: What is the difference between cytosolic and lumen TYRP1? Why are both present on the
MMERF fraction and both susceptible to PK? It would be helpful to include the sample of whole cells
to determine if the two cells have different materials to begin with.
Response: There are no cytosolic or lumenal forms of the protein TYRP1. TYRP1 is a melanosome
membrane protein with domains exposed both to the cytosol and lumen. We took advantage of this
topology and used two different antibodies, each of which could target one of the two differently
exposed regions. This served as a control to ensure that Proteinase K degraded only the cytosolic,
exposed parts of proteins. We have added this explanation to the result section, lines 121-124.
10. Fig 2: It would be necessary to add the lines to B to show the positions of the line scan. F is hard
to see the GFP or magenta signal. The arrows are not helpful.
Response: We revised all the microscopy figures to improve their resolution and visualization.
11. Fig 3. The image quality of A is poor. At the current magnification, it is hard to appreciate if the
arrows indeed point to melanosomes with different morphology in D. It is hard to appreciate the
lumen accumulation of cargo in G. It is not clear what the difference is between the two BF panels in
H.
Response: We have changed all the figures with better resolution and image quality.
12. Scales in Fig S4 are missing or too small to see.
Response: The scale was increased in size; some of these panels are now on Fig.S3 due to changes in
the order, or addition of new panels, in the figures of the manuscript.
13. Typos in lines 79, 215, 293, and figure 1 legend.
Response: These typos were corrected.
Reviewer #2
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part
of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate
recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
Reviewer #3
This study describes a novel role for MFF, or mitochondrial fission factor, in the regulation of
melanosome fission and maturation. The authors begin with a discovery-based platform involving
transcriptomics and proteomics of two cell lines – melan-a cells, which represent a wild-type
melanocyte maturation model, and melan-c2 cells, which harbor a loss-of-function mutation in a key
protein involved in melanogenesis and thus are disrupted in their maturation. The authors preliminarily
find that MFF is enriched in melan-c2 cells, and propose that it localizes to endogenous melanocyte
membranes using immunogold-labeling coupled with EM, as well as fluorescence microscopy. The
authors then find that genetic ablation of MFF, but not the mitochondrial fission factor DRP1, causes
increased early melanosome size and increased intracellular melanin level, which is proposed to reflect
impaired melanocyte maturation. The authors perform RNA-seq on melanocytes harboring MFF
knockdown and find differential expression of ‘catabolism’ proteins, leading the authors to suggest
that MFF activity is required for the removal of unwanted material during maturation. Finally, the
authors perform IP-MS to identify interacting proteins with MFF and identify the ARP2/3 complex,
which they propose is required for MFF-dependent melanosome fission.
While the study has interesting observations, I found many of the conclusions to be overstated and
further find the model for MFF-mediated function at melanosomes unclear. I elaborate on these points
further below.
Major points:
Comment 1: The authors begin their study by “devis[ing] a proteomic pipeline aimed at identifying the
proteins enriched on the surface of the co-sedimenting organelles” – meaning the mitochondria-
melanosome interface. This is a very exciting and interesting proposal, and I was eager to read more
about the technical details about how the authors were able to enrich for mitochondrial-melanosome
interfaces. However, I found that the methods of the “MMERF” isolation as underwhelming, as the
method essentially describes a crude mitochondrial prep. While such a prep would likely contain
“mitochondria-melanosome-ER fractions” or MMERF, as the authors state, it does not provide a
method to “provide a compendium of the proteome of the melanosome-mitochondria interface” as
claimed in line 133. This is simply a heavy membrane fraction in cells in which melanosome maturation
is enabled or impaired. This is not to say that the dataset generated by the authors is not of value; it
is indeed an appropriate experimental approach to identify how mitochondria and mitochondria-
associated proteins differentially accumulate in a model of disrupted melanocyte maturation. The
authors should amend their claim on line 133 mentioned above and render it more reflective of the
dataset collected.
Response: We agree with your observation and have accordingly revised the method description in
the manuscript (line 117-123 and 394-409). However, we would like to emphasize that the novelty of
our approach lies not in the isolation method itself, but in the subsequent digestion step we
introduced. By applying proteinase K digestion to the isolated fractions, we effectively removed
lumenal organellar proteins from consideration, thereby significantly narrowing the pool of potential
candidates involved in mitochondria communication with other organelles in the two models of
melanocytes, focusing only on the proteins that are exposed to the cytosol. We also explored
alternative approaches to isolate mitochondria–melanosome contact sites directly. However, these
attempts were consistently limited by technical challenges, including high levels of contamination with
mitochondria-ER contact sites. To further support our findings, we have now included an additional
dataset based on melanosome immunoprecipitation, which confirms the presence of MFF at
melanosomes regardless of mitochondrial association (Fig. S2D).
2. The authors choose to focus on MFF, which is shown to be enriched in melan-c2 ‘MMERF’ fractions
and is digestable by proteinase K, suggesting it is membrane localized and could be present at an
intraorganellar contact. However, the authors do not provide sufficient rationale for studying MFF
versus other targets. While the claim that MFF is increase in melan-c2 cells is true, Figures 1A and 1B
suggest that most mitochondrial genes are increased in melan-c2 cells. Figure 1D suggests that
mitochondria are larger in melan-c2 cells than melan-a cells, and all mitochondrial targets examined
in Figure 1E are elevated. Why do the authors choose to study MFF in the context of such large
organellar changes across mitochondria?
Response: We are grateful for this feedback, and we acknowledge the need to better support the
rationale. To this aim, we have provided additional quantitative analyses and datasets. First, we
expanded the data originally presented in Fig. S1A/B (now Fig. 1A) and provided new results in Fig. 1B,
1C, and Fig. S1C–E to better highlight the differences in melan-a and melan-c2 related to melanosomes
and mitochondria dynamics. Specifically, we quantified the percentage of melanosomes at various
maturation stages that are in contact with mitochondria in both melan-a and melan-c2 cell lines.
Additionally, we measured the distances between mitochondria and melanosomes at all stages of
maturation, along with the perimeters of each organelle when in contact. To provide a thorough view
of these interactions, we developed a new index—the
Melanosome-Mitochondria Contact Coefficient (MELAMICC)—calculated as follows: MELAMICC = melanosome perimeter / (mitochondria perimeter
× mitochondria–melanosome distance), similar to the ERMICC index, which was previously suggested
for mitochondria-ER contact sites (Naon et al, PNAS 2016). This coefficient provides a normalized
measure of contact, allowing comparison of contact sites across different melanosome stages. Our
findings revealed a significant increase in mitochondria–melanosome contacts in albino melanocytes,
which are also characterized by an accumulation of early-stage melanosomes (Stages I and II). These
observations led us to hypothesize that mitochondria-associated proteins, particularly those exposed
to the cytosol, could play a role in hetero-organelle communication. From our analysis of outer
mitochondrial membrane (OMM) proteins (listed in Fig. 1H), fewer than ten proteins met these
criteria. Among this subset, only three were transcriptionally upregulated in albino melanocytes.
Notably, MFF (Mitochondrial Fission Factor) stood out as particularly intriguing. We further observed
altered expression and specific enrichment of MFF in albino melanocytes, along with increased
melanosome size, suggesting a potential dysfunction in the regulation of their morphology in albino
cells. To investigate this further, we performed additional analyses of melanosome dynamics in melan-
a and melan-c2 (Fig. 1I–K). These data showed a higher number of fission events in early-stage
melanosomes in albino cells than in pigmented controls. We believe this is due to blocked
melanosome maturation and subsequent outgrowth of melanosomes in albino cells, as a
compensatory response to the lack of TYR activity. Given that MFF is a regulator of mitochondria and
peroxisome dynamics, and being the only organelle dynamic protein highlighted by our analyses, we
hypothesized that it could play a role in melanosomal membrane dynamics.
3. In Figure 2, the authors use immunogold staining and fluorescence microscopy to show MFF
proximal to the melanosome membrane, and suggest that MFF co-localizes to sites of melanosome
fission, leading to the claim that “MFF is found on the surface of melanosomes and is present at
melanosome constriction and fission events.” I have questions regarding this claim.
a. The data are not quantified, making them difficult to evaluate. How frequent is MFF presence on
the melanosome membrane? Does this change during differentiation states? How often is MFF found
at melanosome constriction sites? Are there constriction sites that occur that are absent for MFF?
These are important details to understand the necessity of MFF for membrane constriction in this
model system.
Response: To address this relevant point, besides adding the requested quantifications, we have
performed other experiments, now included in Fig. 2 and Fig. S2. Specifically, we quantified how
frequently MFF is present in melanosomes; we found MFF at approximately 20% of HMB45-positive
melanosomes (Fig. 2F). In contrast, the presence of MFF on TYRP1-positive melanosomes (stage III/IV)
was barely detectable (Fig.S2A). Importantly, we did not observe MFF localization at membrane
constriction sites in TYRP1-positive melanosomes, unlike what was observed in those marked by
HMB45. Therefore, we restricted our quantification of MFF at melanosomal constriction sites to the
HMB45-positive population. From this analysis, we concluded that MFF is not universally present at
all melanosome membrane fission sites and is enriched in 22% of observed melanosome membrane
constrictions (Fig. 2I).
b. The authors make a statement in their abstract that their data “unveil an extramitochondrial role
)for MFF in the regulation of melanosome morphology and maturation.” However, the authors have
not demonstrated that MFF is exclusively at the melanosome membrane, rather than a model in which
MFF resides on the mitochondrial membrane but enriches at a melanosome contact site. If the authors
truly believe that MFF is acting in a melanosome-autonomous manner (that is, completely
independent of mitochondrial targeting), more data is required to substantiate this claim.
Response: We understand the concerns raised by the reviewers, and as previously mentioned, we
have included several additional datasets to show that MFF localises to melanosome membranes
regardless of the presence of mitochondria. We have revised Fig. 2 and Fig. S2 in the updated
manuscript. In the newly presented data, we did not observe colocalization of MFF puncta at
melanosomes with either PDH or TOMM20—two well-established mitochondrial markers—thereby
excluding the possibility that these structures are mitochondria or mitochondrial-derived vesicles
(MDVs) (Fig. S2B). Additionally, we generated MELANO-IP melan-a cells to isolate highly purified
melanosome fractions, which were confirmed to be free of mitochondrial contamination (Fig. S2D).
We detected MFF in these purified fractions, while mitochondrial markers were absent, further
supporting that MFF is associated with melanosomes independently of mitochondrial contact.
c. To follow up on point 2b, it is unclear what the authors mean by an “extramitochondrial role” for
MFF. Do the authors propose that MFF independently targets to melanosomes, or that it shuttles
there by way of mitochondria? Or is actually localized on mitochondria but at melanosome contact
sites? The authors should be clearer on their model.
Response: We believe that both scenarios are possible. We observed instances where MFF appears
to bud from mitochondria toward melanosomes (Fig. 2J and Fig. S2G), suggesting a potential direct
transfer. However, we cannot exclude the possibility that cytosolic pools of MFF exist and may also be
trafficked independently to melanosomes. That said, considering that MFF was identified in our
enriched fractions from albino cells, which exhibit increased contact between mitochondria and early-
stage melanosomes, we propose that this organelle proximity may facilitate enhanced MFF trafficking
from mitochondria to melanosomes. To reflect this, we have revised the manuscript text to
acknowledge that both mechanisms should be considered as potential contributors to MFF
localization at melanosomes (line 323-326).
d. The authors repeatedly make claims about the role of MFF in membrane fission, but this is never
shown. Rather, it is inferred that without MFF, melanosomes become enlarged and this could be due
to inefficient organellar fission. The authors should show that MFF directly enables membrane fusion
or soften their language to suggest that this model is consistent with membrane fission, although the
mechanisms by which this occurs are unclear.
Response: We appreciate the reviewers' concerns and have added several new datasets to
demonstrate more clearly the extent of MFF involvement in early melanosome fission. First, using
super-resolution, we observed MFF puncta localizing at the necks of melanosomal tubules, where
membrane constriction and subsequent scission usually occur (as reported for example by Ripoll et al,
2014, Fig. 2H). Additionally, live-cell imaging (Fig. 2K, left panels) shows a single MFF punctum
mediating membrane splitting of a melanosome, with one of the resulting vesicular structures
remaining associated with MFF. A second example (Fig. 2K, right panels) further illustrates the division
of a melanosomal structure into two distinct compartments beneath an MFF punctum. Besides, MFF-
silenced melan-a cells showed a significant reduction in the frequency of melanosome fission events
(Fig. 3H). Considering that MFF is enriched at only ~22% of melanosome membrane constriction sites
(Fig. 2I), these findings suggest that while MFF is not required for all melanosome fission events,
it plays a significant role in facilitating a subset of them. In MFF-depleted cells, fission can still occur,
although at reduced levels. To further clarify the mechanism by which MFF may promote early
melanosome fission, we followed the reviewer’s suggestion and investigated the role of the ARP2/3
complex in melanosome morphology. We performed knockdown experiments targeting two ARP2/3
subunits, ARPC1A and ARPC3, and observed an increase in melanosome size in both cases,
phenocopying the effects of MFF knockdown (Fig. 5G). Importantly, MFF puncta remained detectable
at early-stage melanosomes under these conditions, indicating that MFF recruitment is independent
of the ARP2/3 complex. This supports our model in which MFF may interact with ARP2/3 regulators
to drive fission (Fig. 5H). Finally, to further support the connection between MFF and actin in membrane
dynamics, we show that F-actin is enriched at melanosome fission sites marked by MFF (Fig. 5C,
D), strengthening our hypothesis that MFF-dependent melanosome fission is mediated through localized
actin nucleation.
4. In Figure 3, the authors make the claim that MFF, but not DRP1, is required for melanosome
maturation and function. This is surprising, as the current literature postulates that MFF is solely an
adaptor for DRP1 to mediate mitochondrial membrane fission, but does not have intrinsic membrane
fission capabilities itself. The authors only assay DRP1 knockdown in HMB45 spot perimeter and
number of HMB45 spots per cells in this figure. Is it possible that DRP1 is not sufficiently knocked down
and MFF could be utilizing small amounts of DRP1 to enable differentiation? Does DRP1 ever colocalize
with HMB45 during melanocyte maturation, similar to MFF in Figure 2? Does it ever occur proximal to
HMB45 positive structures via EM, similar to MFF in Figure 2? Further studies should be carried out
with DRP1, as negative data is meaningful in support of the authors’ claims. These experiments also
highlight the importance of quantifying these events for both MFF and DRP1.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful comments. Regarding the efficiency of DRP1 silencing, we
confirm that knockdown was highly effective, with more than 98% reduction observed consistently
across all replicates. This is clearly demonstrated in Fig. 3B and the source data of this figure. Given
this level of knockdown, we believe the residual DRP1 is unlikely to be sufficient to maintain MFF-
dependent melanosome function. As requested, we examined the subcellular localization of both
DRP1 and MFF at melanosomes (Fig. 3A). While we do observe DRP1 on melanosome membranes, we
did not detect any clear colocalization with MFF at these sites, unlike in the case of mitochondria,
where DRP1 and MFF colocalize, as indicated by the orange arrows in Fig. 3A. In contrast, MFF and
DRP1 were detected at distinct regions of the melanosome membrane, as shown by the white and
yellow arrows in Fig. 3A.
To further explore the functional differences between DRP1 and MFF in melanosome biology, we also
analyzed transcriptomic changes following their individual knockdowns. We have now added the RNA-
seq data for DRP1-silenced cells (Fig. 4A). Interestingly, the transcriptional profiles resulting from MFF
and DRP1 knockdowns were markedly distinct. MFF silencing led to the upregulation of pathways
associated with melanosome and lysosome catabolism, consistent with a compensatory response to
disrupted early-stage melanosome dynamics. In contrast, DRP1 silencing resulted in the
downregulation of several key melanosome-specific genes, including MITF, a master regulator of
melanocyte function and melanosome biogenesis. These findings suggest that while both DRP1 and
MFF can localize to melanosomes, their functional roles in this context differ substantially. DRP1 may
influence melanosome gene regulation more broadly (which was previously demonstrated), whereas
MFF appears to play a more specific role in melanosome maturation/ segregation.
5. The authors end the paper by performing IP-MS to identify interaction partners with MFF. However,
the authors do not comment on whether this pulled down MFF associated with melanosomes or
mitochondria. It is likely that the bulk of MFF associates with mitochondria rather than melanosomes,
rendering the stoichiometry and meaning of global MFF interactions presented in this figure unclear.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that the source of the material used for MFF
immunoprecipitation (MFF-IP) should be clearly stated. We have rephrased the relevant section in line
260 and in the methods section for clarity. The MFF-IP was performed using whole-cell lysates from
melan-a cells, not from isolated organelle fractions. We acknowledge that many of the MFF interactors
identified in this experiment may reflect MFF’s known association with mitochondria, rather than
direct interactions at melanosomes. However, when we analysed the enrichment of biological
processes among the identified interactors, we found that the most significantly enriched pathway
was “regulation of ARP2/3 complex-mediated actin nucleation,” as shown in Fig. 5E. Given that
ARP2/3-mediated actin dynamics have previously been implicated in melanosome fission (Ripoll et
al,2018), we consider this the most likely mechanism through which MFF may modulate melanosome
membrane fission. To support this hypothesis, we have performed new experiments and updated Fig.
5 by including the respective results. First, we investigated whether branched F-actin and the ARP2/3
complex are spatially associated with melanosomes using super-resolution immunofluorescence
microscopy. We labelled cells with phalloidin (to visualize F-actin) or an antibody targeting ARPC3 (a
core subunit of the ARP2/3 complex). Both were found to localize at sites of membrane constriction
on melanosomes enriched with MFF (Fig. 5C and Fig.5F). In addition, we performed knockdown
experiments targeting two ARP2/3 subunits, ARPC1A and ARPC3. In both conditions, we observed an
increase in melanosome size, phenocopying the effect seen upon MFF depletion (Fig. 5G). Notably,
MFF puncta remained present at early-stage melanosomes following ARP2/3 complex silencing,
indicating that MFF localization is independent of ARP2/3 complex presence. This finding supports our
interpretation that MFF likely functions in coordination with ARP2/3 regulators, rather than being
recruited by the complex itself, to promote melanosome fission (Fig. 5H).
a. To follow up on point 4 – the authors suggest that “MFF-dependent melanosome fission relies on
ARP2/3 mediated actin assembly”. The authors somewhat suggest that this may be due to different
subunits of the WASH complex, but suggest that phenotypes were not seen due to potential
redundancies and compensation. The authors should use combinatorial knockdowns to explore this
further, as the proposal that DRP1 is not required for membrane fission begs the question of which
molecular components are involved in membrane fission.
Response: We agree with the reviewer, and we have addressed these points with other experiments.
As silencing of Fam21 and Washc5 did not yield significant changes, we decided to target directly the
actin nucleator complex ARP2/3: we found that downregulation of ARPC1A and ARPC3 could mimic
the effect of Mff silencing, supporting their role in melanosome fission (Fig. 5G).
b. Is it possible to further enrich melanosomes specifically and perform the MFF pulldown with this
specific fraction? If many of these hits persist in this experiment, it would suggest that the MFF-ARP2/3
interaction is important specifically at melanosomes, instead of at mitochondria which could indirectly
affect melanosome function.
Response: Thanks for raising this point. Besides isolating pure melanosome fractions (see response to
point 6), we performed co-localization experiments and showed that ARPC3 and F-actin co-localize
with melanosome fission sites marked by MFF (Fig. 5C, D). As pointed out by the reviewer, this data
together and Arpc1a and Arp3 silencing results, suggest that MFF-ARP2/3 interaction is important
specifically at melanosomes.
6. MFF runs as a doublet throughout the western blotting in the manuscript. Is it possible that these
bands represent different MFF isoforms that localize to different organelles? Does this doublet change
in abundance throughout melanocyte maturation? Could the authors purify melanosomes away from
mitochondria and see one versus another isoform of MFF on melanosomes? This could be a very
compelling piece of data that would also address some of the comments raised in point 2 above.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful comments. Indeed, the different bands represent MFF
isoforms. We generate MELANO-IP melan-a cells to isolate highly purified melanosome fractions,
which were confirmed to be free of mitochondrial contamination (Fig. S2D). In these purified fractions,
we detected MFF isoforms curiously differently enriched in melanosome pure fractions (Fig.S2D, E).
We quantified the enrichment level and we observed that isoform 1 was more abundant in the
melanosome pull-down than in the input (whole lysate). In the latter, however, isoform 4 was found
to be more prevalent. We overexpressed all isoforms and quantified HMB45-positive melanosome
size (Fig.S3O). We did not observe any significant changes, but this is perhaps not surprising, as
overexpression alone may be insufficient to drive the phenotype.
Reviewer #4
The manuscript by Rebelo et al. describes a new role for MFF, a mitochondrial fission factor, in
melanosome size and maturation. This is an interesting finding that contributes to the growing body
of evidence on the importance of organelle contacts for melanosome biogenesis, maturation and
function. However, this finding is not entirely novel as mitochondrial-melanosome contacts were
reported 10 years ago by the group of Maria Vittoria Schiaffino. Moreover, this group found that the
mitochondrial protein MFN2 regulates melanosome biogenesis. In terms of mechanism, it is suggested
that MFF-dependent melanosome fission depends on Arp2/3-mediated actin assembly. While this is
interesting, it does not provide enough mechanistic detail for the journal's standard (see point 2).
1 - One major issue is the lack of quantification of melanosome maturation in a manuscript on this
subject. Indeed, authors did not quantify melanosome stages by EM, which is essential to support the
claims made. This applies to several figures in the manuscript, including Fig. S1A/B, 2A - to know if
MFF is present in all melanosome stages in the same proportion - and 3G.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments and agree that the previously missing
quantifications were essential to strengthen our conclusions. We added all the requested
quantifications to the revised manuscript. Specifically, we have included quantifications for the
previous Fig. S1A/B (now Fig. 1A), as shown in Fig. 1B, 1C, and Fig. S1C–E. We quantified the
percentage of melanosomes at different maturation stages that were in contact with mitochondria in
both melan-a and melan-c2 cell lines. We also measured the distances between mitochondria and
melanosomes at all maturation stages, as well mitochondria and melanosome perimeters when in
contact. To provide a thorough view of these interactions, we developed a new index—the
Melanosome-Mitochondria Contact Coefficient (MELAMICC)—calculated as follows: MELAMICC =
melanosome perimeter / (mitochondria perimeter × mitochondria–melanosome distance), similar to
the ERMICC index that was previously suggested for mitochondria-ER contact sites (Naon et al, PNAS
2016). This coefficient provides a normalized measure of contact, allowing comparison of contact sites
across different melanosome stages. Our findings revealed a significant increase in mitochondria–
melanosome contacts in albino melanocytes, which are also characterized by an accumulation of
early-stage melanosomes (Stages I and II). Notably, no mature melanosomes were observed in these
cells, precluding quantification of later stages. To precisely quantify the number of melanosomes
carrying MFF, we then decided to perform super-resolution microscopy experiments (Fig. 2). We
observed that approximately 20% of early-stage melanosomes are positive for MFF (Fig. 2F). Given the
absence of MFF at late-stage melanosomes (TYRP1-positive) and in their constriction sites, these
stages, we focused on early stages. We quantified the number of times that MFF is observed at early
melanosome fission regions (approximately 20% of early-stage melanosomes are positive for MFF)
(Fig. 2I). Lastly, we have now included the quantification of the TEM images shown in the original Fig.
3G (now Fig. 3F), and provided the corresponding graph in Fig. S3M.
2- Another major issue is the use of an inhibitor only to interfere with Arp2/3 and draw conclusions
about the involvement of the complex and actin nucleation. Indeed, pharmacological approaches, as
any other, have pitfalls. Therefore, the findings should be validated with a genetic approach, by
depleting Arp2/3.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion and have now included additional data
addressing the role of the ARP2/3 complex in melanosome morphology. Specifically, we performed
knockdown experiments targeting two different subunits of the ARP2/3 complex, ARPC1A and ARPC3.
In both cases, we observed an increase in melanosome size, consistent with the phenotype seen upon
MFF knockdown (Fig. 5). Notably, MFF puncta remained detectable at early-stage melanosomes under
these silencing conditions, indicating that MFF localizes to melanosomes independently of the ARP2/3
complex itself. This supports our interpretation that MFF may function via interaction with ARP2/3
regulators to facilitate melanosome fission. Furthermore, we immunostained for one ARP2/3 complex
subunit and confirmed its localization to early melanosomes (Fig. S5F, G). To further support the link
between MFF and actin dynamics, we demonstrated the enrichment of F-actin at melanosome fission
sites marked by MFF localisation (see Figures 5C and 5D). This finding reinforces our model that MFF-
dependent melanosome fission is mediated through the localised nucleation of actin.
3 - The evidence that MFF also localizes to stage III and IV melanosomes seems to be largely ignored
by the authors and not considered in the interpretation of the findings.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s observation and agree that MFF localization to later-stage
melanosomes (Stage III and IV) warrants further discussion. Although our super-resolution
microscopy images occasionally revealed MFF signal at these later stages (Fig. 2 and Fig. S2), its
presence was visibly lower compared to early-stage melanosomes. Importantly, we did not observe MFF
enrichment at constriction or fission sites in TYRP1-positive melanosomes, suggesting that MFF may not
be actively involved in fission events at these later maturation stages. To clarify this, we have expanded
the discussion in the revised manuscript. We now consider the possibility that MFF localization to stage
III/IV melanosomes may reflect hybrid or transitional maturation stages that cannot be fully
distinguished using current markers. This could explain partial colocalization. Alternatively, MFF may
serve a different, yet unexplored, role at these stages. However, we did not pursue this possibility as
the focus of our current study was on early melanosomes. Indeed, we initiated our investigation using
an albino melanocyte model that exclusively contains early-stage melanosomes, as it harbours a
Tyrosinase mutation that impedes melanin synthesis. In this model, we observed specific enrichment
and altered expression of MFF. To further support our focus on early-stage melanosomes and MFF,
we included new data quantifying melanosome dynamics in melan-a and melan-c2 cells (Fig. 1I–K).
These analyses revealed an increased number of fission and fusion events in early-stage melanosomes
in albino cells, confirming the presence of altered melanosomal dynamics and supporting a functional
role for MFF in this process.
4 - Regarding the explanation of why Mff-KD cells are more pigmented, it is not likely that immature
melanosomes accumulate melanin (stage II melanosomes should have little pigment). Moreover, a
negative feedback loop is expected to occur, downregulating melanogenesis, and this is likely why the
authors detected lower levels of melanogenic markers. However, this should not lead to increased
pigmentation. Therefore, other mechanisms should be considered.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the increased pigmentation observed in
Mff-KD cells. While we agree that immature melanosomes (e.g., stage II) typically contain little
pigment, we hypothesize that their pigmentation could increase in Mff-silenced cells due to impaired
progression of maturation into later stages. Specifically, we hypothesize that MFF-mediated fission
may participate in the removal of unnecessary material: indeed, similarly to other organelles,
melanosomes must control their size to maintain their homeostasis. Disruption of cargo recycling
could lead to the accumulation of enlarged melanosomal structures, characterized by abnormal
maturation and eventual pigmentation. In line with this idea, we observed: enlarged or doublet
melanosome-like structures in Mff-KD cells (Fig. S3N); a trend toward increased size not only of early
but also of late-stage melanosomes by TEM (Fig. S3M); and a higher colocalization of the early
melanosome marker HMB45 with melanin (Fig. 3I).
Besides, we found that Mff-silenced melanocytes are characterized by a significant upregulation of
lysosomal and catabolic genes, including Ctsb, Ctsd, and Lipa, a transcriptional response not observed
in Drp1-KD cells. Interestingly, unlike Mff, knockdown of Drp1 led to downregulation of the key
melanogenesis regulator Mitf (Fig. 4A), indicating divergent cellular responses to the loss of each
protein.
The specific upregulation of lysosomal enzymes in Mff-KD cells may represent a compensatory
mechanism triggered by impaired melanosome fission, aimed at increasing melanosome degradation
and at limiting the accumulation of enlarged, dysfunctional organelles. However, if this catabolic
response was not sufficient to compensate for the lack of MFF-mediated fission, melanosomes that
are enlarged and only partially mature may persist. Supporting this idea, co-silencing Ctsb with Mff
rescued the elevated melanosomal acidification (Fig. 4H, I), restored the expression of melanogenesis
markers, and further increased both melanin content and melanosome size compared to Mff silencing
alone (Fig. 4J, K; Fig. S4C–J). Moreover, this condition led to a significant accumulation of early-stage
melanosomes per total cell area (Fig. 4L), a phenotype absent in Mff-KD alone (Fig. 3D). These findings
suggest that increased lysosomal enzyme activity, particularly CTSB, contributes to the degradation of
key melanogenic proteins (e.g., TYR, TRP1, GP100), forming part of a negative feedback loop that
attempts to limit melanosome buildup.
And Minor issues:
- Fig. 2G, H does not exist.
Response: We correct this misinformation in the manuscript.
- Reference 8 is old and there are several more recent ones.
Response: We added to the manuscript a more recent reference in addition to reference 8.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have addressed all my concerns.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: This is a revision for a manuscript outlining a role for mitochondrial fission factor (MFF) in the regulation of melanosome fission. The authors have presented a thoughtful response to reviewers, and have satisfactorily addressed my concerns in the first presentation of this manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: The authors thoroughly reviewed the manuscript and considered all the reviewers' comments and suggestions. As a result, the manuscript was vastly improved. Nevertheless, the question of the potential off-target effects was not addressed. Contrary to what the authors state, the use of siRNA pools does not minimize these efects and can even exacerbate them, as four siRNA oligos are present in the pool. Therefore, a rescue experiment is warranted.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewers
Reference number: NCOMMS-24-37754A
We would like to thank the reviewers for their thoughtful evaluations and for acknowledging that the
revised manuscript satisfactorily addresses all points raised during the initial submission. We are
pleased that the reviewers found that the revised work has improved the overall quality and clarity of
the manuscript.
Regarding the remaining concern about potential off-target effects and the suggestion to perform a
rescue experiment, we fully agree that addressing off-target contributions is important. However,
several technical constraints prevented us from accomplishing a definitive rescue.
First, rescue with murine MFF was not feasible because the siRNA pool used in our experiments targets
the mouse MFF coding sequence, as shown in the table provided below (Table 1). This results in rapid
silencing of not only the endogenous, but also the exogenous mouse construct.
Second, although we attempted rescue with two different constructs encoding for human MFF
(tagged either with V5 or with GFP), this strategy was also unworkable: the expression kinetics of the
human construct did not match the siRNA knockdown window, and, critically, one of the siRNA oligos
in the pool also targets human MFF, thereby preventing stable and interpretable rescue (Fig.1).
Third, we tried to generate a stable MFF knockdown cell line, but this approach proved unsuitable for
our model. Indeed, likely due to the primary-like nature of melan-a, after antibiotic selection and cell
expansion the cells showed substantial alterations in cell morphology and pigmentation levels.
Therefore, to address the reviewer’s concerns and independently validate the phenotype while
minimizing off-target effects, we used an alternative knockdown approach. Instead of using a pool of
siRNA, we took advantage of Lentiviral particles carrying an individual shRNA targeting murine MFF.
Specifically, we tested two individual shRNAs. Our Western blot analysis showed that each of these
constructs was able to decrease MFF levels, albeit to a lesser extent than the siRNA pool (Fig.2).
The shRNA that most effectively reduced MFF levels produced a phenotype similar to that observed with
the siRNA pool, although the effect size was smaller (Fig.3). This difference corresponds precisely to
the distinct levels of MFF depletion achieved: our quantifications suggest that the siRNA pool reduces
MFF by ~90–95%, whereas the single shRNA reduces MFF by ~50%. The proportionality between MFF
depletion and phenotypic strength strongly supports the specificity of the effect and argues against
off-target artifacts. Taken together, these results provide evidence that the observed phenotype is
caused by the specific depletion of MFF, rather than by off-target effects.
Overall, we believe that the additional experiments and clarifications provided in the revised
manuscript substantially strengthen the rigour and robustness of our conclusions on the central role
of MFF in regulating melanosome fission by an actin-dependent mechanism. We therefore hope that
you will now consider the manuscript suitable for publication.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Melanosomes are lysosome-related organelles that produce and accumulate melanin. Their maturation is regulated through interactions with mitochondria and involves the export and recycling of proteins via tubular transport and fission events whose mechanisms are unknown. Here, we demonstrate that the mitochondrial fission factor protein (MFF) is involved in melanosome fission. MFF is trafficked between mitochondria and melanosomes and locates at melanosome fission events. Upon downregulation of MFF, but not of dynamin-related protein 1, melanosomes enlarge, intracellular melanin accumulates. melanosomal lumenal catabolism increases, indicating that MFF-dependent melanosomes fission is required for their maturation. We show that MFF interacts with regulators of the ARP2/3 complex, which drives F-actin nucleation. Actin filaments accumulate between melanosomes at MFF-enriched membrane constriction sites, and silencing of ARP2/3 subunits mimicks the increase in melanosome size. MFF regulates actin-dependent fission of melanosomes via the ARP2/3 complex, indicating an extramitochondrial function for MFF in the regulation of melanosome homeostasis.

---

## Introduction

Lysosome-related organelles (LROs) are cell-type-specific organelles of endosomal and/or secretory origin that share adaptive physiological functions, morphological features, and cargoes. Pigmented cells such as epidermal melanocytes and retinal pigment epithelial cells contain melanosomes, a type of LRO that allows compartmentalization of synthesis and storage of melanin pigments 1,2.

Melanosomes share several features with lysosomes. These include acidic intraluminal pH, the presence of lysosomal membrane proteins, luminal proteases, and hydrolases, including cathepsins 3-5. Even so, melanosome identity is determined by the presence of specific melanogenesis-associated machinery, such as the pre-melanosome protein (GP100; also known as PMEL17), Tyrosinase (TYR), and Tyrosinase-related proteins 1 and 2 (TYRP1/TYRP2) 6.

Melanosomes have been proposed to arise from endosomes and multivesicular bodies (MVBs). They are classified into four different stages of maturation based on distinct morphological features. Stage I melanosomes (pre-melanosomes or early melanosomes) are unpigmented endosomal-like compartments lacking melanogenic enzymes and characterized by luminal membranous vesicles 7. Stage II melanosomes exhibit an ellipsoidal shape with striae, due to the presence of GP100 that assembles into amyloidogenic fragments and then into parallel longitudinal fibers within the lumen of the organelle. Stage III melanosomes contain melanogenic enzymes like TYR and TYRP1/2 and visible melanin deposition onto GP100 scaffold/structured sheets. Stage IV melanosomes are fully pigmented and, under physiological conditions, move to the cell periphery where they are secreted and subsequently taken up by keratinocytes8,9 .

The maturation of melanosomes occurs upon delivery/export of melanogenic proteins through the endolysosomal recycling pathway. In line with their endosomal lineage, melanosomes appear to have the plastic and dynamic capacity to undergo homotypic fusion and fission through tubular and/or vesicular membrane remodeling10-16.

This idea is supported by the evidence that myosin 6 (MYO6), along with optineurin (OPTN), Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog (WASH), and the actin-related protein 2/3 (ARP2/3)-dependent actin nucleation complex participate in melanosome membrane constriction and fission events 15. Specifically, MYO6 mediates the severing of vesicle-associated membrane protein 7 (VAMP7)-positive tubule necks emerging from melanosome membrane subdomains. This process allows the export of non-essential components and fosters proper melanosome maturation 15. Modulators of phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate (PI(3,5)P2) levels, like the kinase PIKfyve, also promote the formation and release of membrane tubules from early melanosomes 17. Therefore, it is likely that different types of machinery regulate melanosome membrane remodeling, depending on the maturation stage.

Mitochondria supply ATP and calcium (Ca2+) to support melanosome maturation and melanin synthesis 18-20. Early-stage melanosomes have been shown to interact more with mitochondria19. Two possible explanations could account for this evidence. First, the proximity between organelles could facilitate the entry of ATP into the melanosomes, thereby fostering melanin synthesis and their maturation; second, it could support the recruitment of specific mitochondrial proteins to the melanosome surface during melanogenesis. Which would be the case still needs to be clarified.

Mitochondria and melanosomes are physically in contact through the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) protein mitofusin 2 (MFN2) that regulates mitochondria-melanosome apposition in space and time during active melanogenesis19. Whether the communication between these two organelles extends beyond the established role of MFN2 is unknown, despite mounting evidence for the role of mitochondria contact sites in several cellular processes, like Ca2+ homeostasis, lipid metabolism, and organelle function and dynamics.

While investigating the role of the mitochondrial proteome in melanosome function, we found that the mitochondrial fission factor (MFF) is present on the surface of melanosomes, independently of mitochondria. MFF localization on the melanosome surface enables it to interact with components of the ARP2/3 complex, facilitating early melanosome fission without its mitochondrial pro-fission partner DRP1. The promotion of maturation, and for their function during melanogenesis.

---

## Results

Comparison of pigmented and albino melanocytes identifies MFF involvement in mitochondria-melanosomes crosstalk
To clarify the role of the interaction between mitochondria and melanosomes, we compared wild-type (melan-a) and albino (melan-c2) melanocytes, which lack melanin due to a loss-of-function mutation in the Tyr gene (Fig. S1A, B). These cells lack melanin synthesis, which in turn blocks melanosome maturation and causes an accumulation of early-stage melanosomes (stages I and II).

Given the abnormal accumulation of immature melanosomes in albino cells compared to pigmented cells, we reasoned that mitochondria-early melanosome communication could also be altered. In line with this idea, our analysis confirmed that albino cells accumulate early-stage melanosomes (I/II) and are characterized by increased contact sites with mitochondria (Fig. 1A, B). We observed that, as they mature, melanosomes appear closer to mitochondria, with this proximity being significantly greater in albino cells at stage I than in pigmented cells. (Fig. 1C). In parallel we performed a differential expression analysis on the two cell lines using RNA-seq and found a significant upregulation of mitochondrial genes in albino cells compared to pigmented ones (Fig. 1D, E; Fig. S1FR; Supplementary Data 1).

Then, we isolated mitochondria-melanosome-ER fractions (MMERF) from melan-a and melan-c2 cells and analyzed them by mass spectrometry (MS) (Fig. 1F, G and “Methods” section). To identify membrane-bound proteins involved in mitochondria-organelle interactions, we subjected MMERFs to limited proteolysis (Fig. 1F, G; Fig. S1G). Proteins identified in both treated and untreated fractions were considered luminal, being protected from the added proteases. To confirm which proteins were exposed on the surface of organelles, we exploited the topology of TYRP1. TYRP1 is a melanosome membrane protein with domains facing either the cytosol or the organelle lumen. We used two different antibodies, each of which could target one of the two regions with different exposure. This served as a control to ensure that proteinase K degraded only the exposed, cytosolic parts of proteins (Fig 1L) . Proteins identified only in the untreated MMERF fractions were considered to be exposed to the organelle surfaces due to their susceptibility to proteolysis (Fig. 1F, G, L, and Fig. S1G). A Venn diagram of the proteomic datasets obtained from the two cell lines revealed 109 common proteins, with 136 enriched in melan-a and 242 in melan-c2 (Fig. 1H; Supplementary Data 2). Functional annotation showed that MMERFs from melan-a were enriched in Golgi and proteasome-related proteins, while MMERFs from melan-c2 contained more lysosomal, ER, and outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) proteins (Fig. 1F). The list of OMM candidates included proteins previously retrieved at mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDVs), membrane contact sites (CTP1A, FUNDC2, MAVS, MTOR, RHOT2, TOM20, TOM34, TOM70) 21 and, unexpectedly, the mitochondrial fission factor MFF.

Although we could not observe morphological differences in the mitochondria network between healthy and pigmented melanocytes (Fig. SI1J, K), we noticed that albino melanocytes were characterized not only by an accumulation of early melanosomes, but also by an increased size of the organelles (Fig. S1J-M). Therefore, we conducted a thorough examination to determine whether there were any changes in melanosome dynamics between the two cell lines (Fig. 1I). Using Lysotracker to monitor melanosome dynamics as done previously22,23, we observed that, despite having larger melanosomes, albino cells showed more fission events (Fig. 1I, J, K). Interestingly, fusion events in albino cells were also more frequent (Fig. S1O, P). These results suggested that the loss of function of TYR in albino cells leads to defective melanosome dynamics: in these cells, melanosome fusion rates would be outpaced by fission due to the inability to progress with melanin synthesis and with maturation of the organelles. Since MFF has been implicated in the division of different organelles, not only mitochondria, we hypothesized that it could participate in melanosome maturation.

MFF can bud from mitochondria to melanosomes and resides at melanosome constriction sites
MFF serves as a membrane adaptor for the dynamin-like GTPase DRP1 in mitochondria and peroxisomal division 24-26. Hence, MFF is also present in non-mitochondrial locations, where it facilitates membrane fission27. We investigated MFF localization using immunogold electron microscopy. MFF was present at the surface of melanosomes at every stage of maturation, independent of the presence of nearby mitochondria (Fig. 2A). To further confirm MFF localization, we used super-resolution microscopy in cells that have been labelled with HMB45, a monoclonal antibody that marks early melanosomes, recognizing an epitope of the protein GP100. Following synthesis, GP100 is subject to several proteolysis steps, resulting in its conversion into the HMB45-reactive low molecular weight form (∼35 kDa)28. This form is known to associate with the fibrillar content of melanosomes: as melanin is produced and deposited on the fibrillar matrix, the HMB45-reactive epitopes gradually become covered, and by the time melanosomes mature into Stage III, reactivity with HMB45 is lost 28. We found MFF-positive puncta at the surface of melanosomes both in melan-a and melan-c2 melanocytes (Fig. 2B, C, D, E). MFF puncta were not positive for TOMM20 or PDH, excluding the possibility of being part of mitochondria or MDVs (Fig. S2B). At steady state, approximately 22% of melanosomes marked by HMB45 were found to have MFF puncta in melan-a cells (Fig. 2F). Some MFF puncta colocalized with the mature melanosome marker TRP1, though to a lesser extent than with HMB45 (Fig. S2A). Quantitative analysis revealed that MFF and mtRFP colocalized less in albino melanosomes compared to pigmented melanocytes, suggesting a larger pool of non-mitochondrial MFF in albino cells (Fig. 2G). Consistent with this, we observed increased colocalization of MFF with HMB45 in albino melanocytes (Fig. S2C). Endogenous MFF was detected not only on the melanosome surface but also at membrane constriction sites and in vesicular/tubular extensions of early melanosomes (Fig. 2H). Quantitative analysis indicated that MFF was associated with approximately 25% of the observed melanosomal fission regions (Fig. 2I), suggesting that there may be distinct fission sites as reported also for other organelles29. Therefore, we sought to understand whether MFF is directly involved in melanosome fission. First, we generated melan-a MELANO-IP cells, and then we verified the presence of MFF in pure melanosomal fractions, free of mitochondrial contamination (Fig. S2D, E). We found that isoform 1 of MFF was enriched in melanosomal fractions, whereas isoform 4 appeared more enriched in the total input (Fig. S2D, E). Overexpression of eGFP-MFF isoform 1 confirmed its localization at HMB45-positive structures and fission sites (Fig. S2F). To verify how MFF could be delivered to melanosomes, we performed time-lapse experiments by marking them with LAMP1-RFP, which had been previously found enriched in these organelles30 and which co-localized with HMB45 in melan-a (Fig. 2B).

With this approach, we observed eGFP-MFF isoform 1 budding from mitochondria and moving toward LAMP1-RFP-positive structures (Fig. 2J). This result was also confirmed by staining stage I/II melanosomes, which have an acidic lumen, with Lysotracker (Fig. S2G). Of note, although we had evidence of MFF being trafficked from mitochondria to melanosomes, we cannot exclude the possibility that cytosolic pools of MFF exist, which may also be independently targeted to these organelles. Super-resolution time-lapse imaging highlighted the presence of MFF puncta at the neck of melanosome tubules, with membrane constriction and scission occurring at or near MFF puncta (Fig. 2K). Figure 2K shows that melanosome membranes can be split into two separate vesicular structures by an MFF punctum, with which they can remain attached (left example) or be released (Fig. 2K, right example). These results demonstrate that MFF associates with melanosomes and that it is enriched at fission sites independently of mitochondrial proximity, likely facilitating melanosome membrane fission.

MFF depletion disrupts melanosome fission and promotes lysosomal protease-mediated degradation
Melanosomes have previously been shown to undergo vesicular and tubular fission, a mechanism critical for regulating their composition and function15. Thus, considering our results, we hypothesized that the recruitment of MFF to the melanosome surface may control their maturation by mediating fission events. Given that MFF is a known receptor for DRP1 (dynamin-related protein 1) - the GTPase responsible for mitochondrial membrane fission—we assessed if Drp1 could be involved in MFF-mediated melanosome fission. We investigated the potential colocalisation of DRP1 and MFF in melan-a cells. Using immunofluorescence, we detected DRP1 at the melanosome surface, similarly to MFF. However, minimal to no colocalization between the two proteins was observed at melanosomes (Fig. 3A). To further explore their eventual function in melanogenesis, we performed siRNA-mediated knockdown (KD) of both Mff and Drp1 in wild-type melanocytes (Fig. 3B; Fig. S3A, B). Interestingly, knocking down either gene led to reduced expression of melanogenic proteins (Fig. S3C-E). However, while intracellular melanin levels were slightly reduced in Drp1-KD cells, they were significantly increased in Mff-KD cells (Fig. S3F). This increase in melanin could be explained by either enhanced melanin synthesis or the accumulation of dysfunctional, immature melanosomes. Given the reduced levels of melanogenic markers, we excluded the former and focused on the possibility of impaired melanosome maturation. Using SR microscopy, we observed that HMB45-positive melanosomes were enlarged only in Mff-silenced melan-a cells (Fig. 3C). The number of HMB45-positive melanosomes remained unchanged in both knockdown conditions (Fig. 3D), but the melanosomes were significantly larger only in Mff-silenced cells (Fig. 3E; Fig. S3H). TEM further confirmed that Mff-KD cells harbored larger melanosomes, often connected by narrow, neck-like structures, or appearing as a fusion of melanosomes at different maturation stages (Fig. 3F; Fig. S3L, M). The presence of these hybrid early–late stage melanosomes suggests the inability to complete fission and that melanogenesis does not progress properly in the absence of MFF. Indeed, we observed a significantly lower frequency of fission events in Mff-KD cells compared to controls (Fig. 3G, H). Additionally, the colocalization of pigmented melanin granules (visible in brightfield) with HMB45-positive melanosomes was significantly higher in Mff-KD cells, further supporting the presence of hybrid melanosomal structures (Fig. 3I, J).

Interestingly, despite reduced fission frequency, melanosomal fission was not entirely abolished in Mff-silenced melanocytes. This is consistent with previous observations that MFF is not present at all visible melanosomal constriction sites (Fig. 2I), and it suggests that alternative fission mechanisms may exist.

To test whether MFF overexpression could influence melanosome morphology, we overexpressed all four MFF isoforms and assessed melanosome size (Fig. S3O). MFF overexpression alone was insufficient to promote melanosome fragmentation, supporting that MFF is not the sole mediator of melanosome division.

Defective melanosome membrane remodeling and fission result in increased melanosome size and accumulation of undegraded or unnecessary proteins, ultimately leading to impaired melanogenesis 15,17. To better understand how MFF and DRP1 depletion differentially impact melanosome homeostasis, we performed RNA sequencing on Mff- and Drp1-silenced melanocytes. Mff silencing led to the upregulation of genes associated with the homeostasis of lysosomes (Capn2, Ctsb, Ctsd, Dpp7, Gabarap, Kxd1, Lipa, Lrrc8a, Mfsd12, Mt1, Myo5a, Plekhm2, Rab7b, Scarb2, Siae, Sidt2, Tpcn1, Tpp1), melanosomes (Capg, Ctsb, Ctsd, Mfsd12, Myh11, Myo5a, Tpp1, Trpv2, Kxd1) or both (Ctsb, Ctsd, Mfsd12) (Supplementary Data 3). These transcriptional changes were not observed in Drp1-silenced cells, which instead showed a broad downregulation of key melanogenesis regulators, including Microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) (Fig. 4A; Supplementary Data 3). These findings confirm that Mff and Drp1 silencing have distinct functional consequences in pigmented cells. While Mff-KD triggers the upregulation of lysosomal and catabolic genes, including cathepsins (Ctsb, Ctsd) and lysosomal lipase (Lipa), Drp1-KD primarily alters melanocyte differentiation and pigment production by downregulating transcriptional regulators such as MITF. As to the specific upregulation of lysosomal/catabolic genes in Mff-KD, we hypothesized that this response may reflect a compensatory mechanism triggered by impaired melanosome fission. Supporting this, CTSB protein levels were elevated in Mff-silenced melanocytes, which showed an increased colocalization of CTSB and HMB45-positive melanosomes (Fig. 4B–E). CTSB enzymatic activity was also significantly increased in Mff-KD cells (Fig. 4F, G). These data suggest that MFF depletion promotes the trafficking and activity of lysosomal enzymes like CTSB, which are key in the process of melanosomes degradation31,32. Their enhanced melanosome localization could be potentially due to either increased melanosome–lysosome fusion or increased trafficking of lysosomal hydrolases, resulting in their partial conversion to a lysosome-like state. Both scenarios are consistent with a shift toward increased melanosome degradation, which is likely a compensatory response to blocked fission. To confirm this hypothesis, we assessed melanosomal acidification, a hallmark of lysosomal activity and of early melanosome, whose pH undergoes neutralization during maturation. Acidification was significantly increased in Mff-KD cells, but it was rescued to control levels by co-silencing CTSB (Fig. 4H, I). Notably, combined silencing of Mff and Ctsb restored the expression of melanogenesis markers (downregulated in Mff-KD alone) and further increased both melanin content and melanosome size, compared to Mff silencing alone (Fig. 4J, K, and Fig. S4C-I). Consequently, when CTSB-mediated melanosomal degradation was suppressed in Mff-KD cells, a marked accumulation of early-stage melanosomes was observed per total cell area (Fig. 4L), which was not detected in Mff silencing alone (Fig. 3D). These findings indicate that the degradation of key melanogenic proteins (such as TYR, TRP1, and GP100) is enhanced in Mff-KD cells due to increased recruitment and activity of lysosomal enzymes within the melanosome lumen. This could represent a negative feedback mechanism aimed at reducing melanosome buildup when fission is impaired.

In summary, MFF depletion impairs early-stage melanosome maturation and triggers a compensatory upregulation of lysosomal catabolism to prevent the accumulation of dysfunctional or oversized melanosomes in response to decreased DRP1-independent melanosome fission.

MFF-dependent melanosome fission requires ARP2/3-mediated F-actin assembly
Our data suggest that MFF can modulate the maturation of melanosomes by controlling their membrane fission independently of DRP1. To shed light on the molecular mechanisms of MFF-mediated melanosome fission, we determined the MFF interactome by immunoprecipitating it from melan-a whole cell lysate and identified the co-purified proteins by MS (Supplementary Data 3). The list of interacting proteins was enriched in actin cytoskeleton organization regulators, including subunits of the WASH core complex (Fig. 5A). This complex functions as an actin nucleation-promoting factor at the surface of endosomes and melanosomes, recruiting the ARP2/3 complex and allowing actin polymerization for vesicle/tubule fission 15,33. FAM21C and Strumpellin (Kiaa0196) are key members of the WASH complex that appeared as hits from our IP (Fig. 5A). After confirming their interaction with MFF (Fig. 5B) and close apposition with early and late-stage melanosomes (Fig. S5G), we verified if their downregulation could affect early melanosome morphology (Fig. S5A, B, C). In melan-a cells, depletion of either of the two leads to no significant changes (Fig.S5D, E). These results suggest that the different components of the complex may have redundant functions and may compensate for each other. A gene ontology (GO) analysis of the MFF interactome also highlighted that the actin nucleation complex may be involved in MFF function (Fig. 5C). Therefore, to clarify the contribution of actin filaments to MFF-mediated melanosome fission, we co-stained melan-a expressing eGFP-MFF with phalloidin and HMB45 (Fig. 5D). We observed F-actin at and in between MFF-positive melanosome constriction sites (Fig. 5D,E). Because ARP2/3 complex-mediated actin nucleation was among the enriched GO terms (Fig. 5C), we sought to understand whether the effect of MFF depends on the ARP2/3 complex by silencing two different subunits: ARPC1A and ARPC3 (Fig. S5H-J). Their silencing led to increased early melanosome size, which was more noticeable when ARPC1A was silenced (Fig. 5F). ARPC1A silencing also led to a change in intracellular melanin levels (Fig. S5K. Besides, we confirmed ARP2/3 complex subunit localization at MFF-HMB45-positive melanosomes (Fig. 5G), and we found that MFF puncta locate in proximity to the enlarged melanosomes in ARPC1A/ARPC3-silenced cells (Fig. S5L). This evidence suggests that the recruitment of MFF to melanosomes is independent of the ARP2/3 complex. Silencing of MFF led to increased melanosome size, consistent with a role in promoting organelle fission. However, co-treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 (a small molecule that stabilizes the ARP2/3 complex in its inactive state and thereby blocks actin nucleation) abrogated this phenotype, suggesting that melanosome enlargement in the absence of MFF requires active actin polymerization (Fig. 5H).
